2026-01-01T17:42:04.0046240Z **DNA Study of 117-Year-Old Woman Sheds New Light on Long Life**
2026-01-01T17:42:04.0058416Z Scientists studied the DNA and biological samples of Maria Branyas, who died at age 117 in 2024 and was the world’s oldest living person at the time of her death. Researchers at the Josep Carreras Leukaemia Research Institute in Barcelona analyzed her blood, saliva, urine, and stool samples using advanced genetic and biological methods. Despite her chronological age of 117, her cells exhibited characteristics typical of much younger individuals. Her genome included rare genetic variants linked to strong immune function, cardiovascular health, and brain resilience. Physiologically, she had very low inflammation, excellent heart health markers, a youthful gut microbiome, and favorable lipid profiles—low 'bad' cholesterol and triglycerides, and high 'good' cholesterol. A surprising finding was the extreme shortening of her telomeres, which usually correlate with higher disease risk, yet she remained free of major age-related illnesses throughout her life. Researchers speculate that such short telomeres may have suppressed cancer development. The study, published in Cell Reports Medicine, emphasizes that advanced age and poor health are not inherently linked, as Branyas’s biological profile defied typical ageing expectations. While lifestyle factors such as a Mediterranean diet, physical activity, and social engagement may have contributed, genetics likely played a major role. Researchers caution that findings from a single individual cannot be generalized without further study. Branyas’s biological legacy offers a unique opportunity to investigate healthy longevity in centenarians and supercentenarians.

2026-01-01T17:42:04.0072015Z **Americans in 1998 tried to predict 2025. Here's what they got right**
2026-01-01T17:42:04.0077175Z In 1998, Gallup and USA Today surveyed 1,055 Americans via landline phones to predict life in 2025. Most correctly anticipated that a Black president would be elected (Barack Obama served from 2009–2017), that gay marriage would become legal and common (legalized nationwide in 2015), and that a deadly new disease would emerge (referring to the COVID-19 pandemic). However, predictions that space travel would be common for ordinary Americans or that alien life would make contact were deemed incorrect. About two-thirds expected a female president by 2025, but no woman has yet been elected. Over half expected a cure for cancer, and 61% believed people would routinely live to 100 years old—neither of which has materialized. The poll also revealed widespread pessimism: 70% believed quality of life would improve for the rich, but most expected worsening conditions for the poor; nearly 80% anticipated less personal privacy, 57% expected less personal freedom, and a 71% majority thought raising good children would be harder. Despite these concerns, most believed race relations would improve and medical care would be more available, albeit less affordable. In 1998, 60% of Americans were satisfied with the country’s direction; by 2026, that number had dropped to 24%, according to Gallup. The original predictions are archived at the Roper Center at Cornell University.

2026-01-01T17:42:04.0082615Z **1998 Americans' Predictions for 2025: Five Correct, Three Unfulfilled**

2026-01-01T17:42:04.0090331Z **DNA Study of 117-Year-Old Woman Reveals Clues to Long Life**
2026-01-01T17:42:04.0096592Z Maria Branyas, who lived to 117 years old and was the oldest living person in the world at her death in 2024, provided biological samples—including blood, saliva, urine, and stool—before her passing. A study led by scientists at the Josep Carreras Leukaemia Research Institute in Barcelona found that her genome exhibited signs of exceptional youthfulness, with cells behaving as though they were significantly younger than her chronological age. Despite a 'huge erosion' of telomeres—typically associated with aging—her immune system, gut microbiome, cardiovascular health, and lipid profile were remarkably favorable, showing low inflammation, low 'bad' cholesterol and triglycerides, and high 'good' cholesterol. Her health was marked by excellent cardiovascular function and mental, social, and physical activity throughout life. The researchers, including epigeneticists Eloy Santos-Pujol and Aleix Noguera-Castells, suggest that her extreme longevity may be due to a combination of rare genetic variants linked to longevity, immune function, and heart and brain health. Notably, the study challenges the conventional role of telomeres as aging biomarkers, proposing that short telomeres might have helped prevent cancer in her case. The findings, published in *Cell Reports Medicine*, offer new insights into healthy aging and potential strategies to extend life expectancy, though the team acknowledges the limitations of studying only one supercentenarian and calls for larger cohort studies. Branyas exceeded the average life expectancy for women in Catalonia by over 30 years, underscoring that advanced age and poor health are not inherently linked.

2026-01-01T17:42:04.0285747Z **Predicting the future: The supergroup of AI, humans, hedgehogs and foxes**
2026-01-01T17:42:04.0291783Z Philip Tetlock, a psychology professor and author of *Superforecasting*, explains how his research on expert prediction has evolved to include large language models (LLMs).  In the 1980s he launched a prediction tournament that showed most experts performed no better than random guessing, but a minority—"foxes" who used diverse information and Bayesian updating—outperformed the "hedgehogs" who stuck to a single thesis.  Tetlock’s later work, the Good‑Judgement Project (GJP), demonstrated that teams of superforecasters beat a control group by 60 % in year 1 and 78 % in year 2, and outperformed university teams by 30‑70 %.  He then tested LLM assistants: participants using a super‑forecasting‑trained LLM improved their accuracy by 28 % overall and 41 % when the outlier question was removed, compared with a control model.  A separate experiment found that the aggregate forecast of a diverse “silicon crowd” of LLMs was statistically indistinguishable from that of a human crowd, though still 30 % below the performance of super‑forecaster teams.  Tetlock concludes that LLMs can act as counterfactual generators, fermize problems, and provide a “wisdom of the silicon crowd,” potentially becoming super‑forecasters themselves within 2‑5 years.  He stresses that forecasting is a better test of AI intelligence than standard exams, and that LLMs’ lack of a fixed worldview may be advantageous for exploring unknown futures.  Key quotes include: 'It is absolutely crucial to integrate LLMs into almost all lines of inquiry,' says Tetlock, and 'Superforecasters could predict out 300 days with the same accuracy as ordinary predictors could predict 100 days.'
